Bedstead
BED-sted
noun
From bed and the Old English stede, “a place, a standing, that whereon a thing stands”; hence the frame that bears a bed. In the KJV it occurs but once, of the iron bedstead of Og king of Bashan.

Biblical Definition

A bedstead is the frame or standing-place of a bed — the bedframe, as distinguished from the bedding laid upon it. The word occurs once only in all the Authorized Version, and it is a hapax with a giant in it: “For only Og king of Bashan remained of the remnant of giants; behold, his bedstead was a bedstead of iron… nine cubits was the length thereof, and four cubits the breadth of it, after the cubit of a man” (Deu 3:11). Moses is writing history, not fable. Og was a real king who came out to real battle at Edrei (Deu 3:1), whose coast is surveyed among the conquered lands (Jos 12:4), and whose overthrow Israel sang for a mercy that endureth for ever. He was of the remnant of the Rephaim, and his iron bedframe — some thirteen feet by six — was kept at Rabbath of the children of Ammon as a relic any man might go and measure. The Spirit gives the dimensions precisely because the thing could be checked. The bedstead preaches two doctrines at once. First, that the LORD is not hindered by stature: the giant whose bedframe was a wonder fell before a people who had no iron at all, for the battle is the LORD’s. Second, that greatness of body is no defence against the judgment of God. Og lay down at last on a bed he could not carry with him, and the iron frame outlived the king who slept on it.

Webster 1828 Definition

The frame or standing-place that bears a bed; in Deuteronomy, the iron bedframe of Og king of Bashan.

BEDSTEAD, a frame for supporting a bed; the standing-place of a bed.

From bed and the Saxon stede, “a place, a standing.”

A KJV hapax, occurring but once (Deu 3:11).

Og’s bedstead was of iron, nine cubits long and four broad, kept at Rabbath.

It witnesses to the real stature of a real king of the Rephaim.

Key Scripture

Deu 3:11 — "For only Og king of Bashan remained of the remnant of giants; behold, his bedstead was a bedstead of iron; is it not in Rabbath of the children of Ammon? nine cubits was the length thereof, and four cubits the breadth of it, after the cubit of a man."

Deu 3:1 — "Then we turned, and went up the way to Bashan: and Og the king of Bashan came out against us, he and all his people, to battle at Edrei."

Jos 12:4 — "And the coast of Og king of Bashan, which was of the remnant of the giants, that dwelt at Ashtaroth and at Edrei,"

Amo 6:4 — "That lie upon beds of ivory, and stretch themselves upon their couches, and eat the lambs out of the flock, and the calves out of the midst of the stall;"

Modern Corruption

The live misuse is the reflex that files Og among legends because his bedstead was nine cubits long; Moses gives the measurements precisely because the thing could be measured.

expand to see more

There is a live misuse here, and it is the modern reflex that hears “nine cubits” and quietly reclassifies Og as folklore, a giant borrowed from the tales of the nations and dressed in Israelite clothes. The canonical narrative does not permit it. Moses names the king, the kingdom, the city of the battle, the tribe he sprang from, and the town where the relic was kept — is it not in Rabbath of the children of Ammon? — and then gives the length and the breadth after the common cubit of a man, the very details a man supplies when he expects to be checked. Joshua surveys Og’s coast among the lands actually taken; the psalms sing his fall among the LORD’s real mercies. To call this legend is not humility before the evidence; it is unbelief dressed as caution. The spade of the archaeologist may corroborate Scripture, but it never sits in judgment on Scripture: the Word of God is the authority, and the dust is the witness.

The second temptation runs the other way — to make Og a curiosity, a wonder for the museum, and to miss the doctrine in the bedframe. The Spirit did not record the iron for our amusement. Israel had no iron and no stature, and the LORD delivered the giant into their hand, that no flesh should glory in His presence. And Og, whose bedstead was a marvel to measure, died like a man and left his frame behind him. Amos knew the same lesson from the other end: they that lie upon beds of ivory and stretch themselves upon their couches shall go captive with the first that go captive. Whether the bed be iron or ivory, no man carries it through the judgment, and the LORD who felled the last of the Rephaim is not impressed by the size of anyone.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means the frame or standing-place that bears a bed.

Bedstead — from bed + Old English stede, “a place, a standing.”

It denotes the frame that bears the bed, not the bedding itself.

A KJV hapax, occurring only in Deu 3:11.

Og’s was of iron, nine cubits by four, kept as a relic at Rabbath.

It witnesses to a real king of the Rephaim, really judged by God.

Usage

"Og’s bedstead was of iron, nine cubits long — Moses gives the measure because it could be measured."

"The giant fell before a people without iron: the battle is the LORD’s, not the tallest man’s."

"Iron bed or ivory couch, no man carries his bedstead through the judgment of God."
